#4295. Global fossil fuel emissions set to fall in 2026, but total CO2 keeps rising

Global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to decline slightly in 2026, offering a promising sign that the world's transition to cleaner energy is beginning to make a measurable difference. According to the latest Global Carbon Budget from the Global Carbon Project, fossil fuel CO2 emissions are projected to fall by 0.4%, partly because of growing solar and wind power generation and disruptions linked to the Iran conflict.

The report estimates that fossil fuel emissions will total 38.2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) in 2026. Oil emissions alone are expected to drop by 1.9%, largely reflecting a temporary energy shock associated with the conflict.

Clean energy is also playing an increasingly important role. Although worldwide energy consumption continues to grow, solar power, wind power, and electric vehicles are now meeting roughly two-thirds of the additional demand. Even so, researchers caution that the transition is not happening quickly enough to guarantee a lasting reduction in fossil fuel emissions.

Fossil Fuel Emissions Fall, but Total CO2 Keeps Rising

Despite the projected decline in fossil fuel emissions, the overall picture is more troubling. When emissions from land-use change (such as deforestation) are included, total global CO2 emissions are expected to reach 43.3 billion metric tons in 2026, compared with 42.8 billion metric tons in 2025.

That increase highlights how progress in cleaner energy can be undermined by continued forest loss and other changes to the landscape.

The report also delivers a stark warning about the world's remaining carbon budget (the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before warming reaches 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels). Researchers estimate that just 150 billion metric tons remain, enough for less than four years at today's emission rates.

As carbon dioxide continues accumulating in the atmosphere, the risks and damaging consequences of climate change are becoming more severe.

Natural Carbon Sinks Face New Climate Pressures

Beyond tracking emissions, the researchers examined the planet's natural "sinks" (absorption of CO2 by land and ocean). These natural systems help limit atmospheric carbon dioxide by taking up some of what human activities release.

The amount of carbon absorbed by land ecosystems has recovered to earlier levels after weakening substantially during the 2023-24 El Niño weather pattern. However, scientists expect the powerful 2026 El Niño to significantly influence carbon absorption in the coming year.

The research brought together experts from the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich (LMU), the Alfred-Wegener-Institut, and more than 90 additional institutions worldwide.

Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, who directs the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter and led the research, emphasized that a temporary reduction in emissions is not enough.

"A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution."

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline."

Clean Energy Could Bring a Historic Turning Point

Despite the challenges, researchers see growing evidence that renewable energy and electric transportation are beginning to change the trajectory of global emissions.

Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society Research Professor at UEA's School of Environmental Sciences, pointed to the expanding influence of clean technologies, particularly in China.

"Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years."

However, a single year of falling emissions does not necessarily mean the world has reached a lasting peak. Glen Peters, Research Professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, stressed the importance of changes that permanently reduce reliance on fossil fuels.

"A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles is pushing emissions down in dozens of countries and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions."

Researchers also emphasize that reducing emissions alone will not be sufficient. Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere must become a much larger part of climate strategies.

Professor Julia Pongratz of LMU's Department of Geography explained the challenge:

"Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO2 removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO2, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now."

Carbon Emissions in China, the US, India, and Europe

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget reveals significant differences in how emissions are changing across major economies.

China, which accounts for approximately 32% of the world's fossil fuel emissions, is expected to record a 0.9% reduction in 2026 after two consecutive years of relatively slow emissions growth. A substantial decline in oil emissions is helping drive the decrease, although emissions from coal are projected to rise slightly by 0.3%.

At the same time, China continues rapidly expanding electricity generation from renewable sources. The country leads the world in deploying clean technologies and expanding carbon absorption through reforestation. About half of the emissions avoided globally through renewable energy and electric vehicles can be attributed to China. It also has the largest carbon uptake from reforestation and afforestation (new forests).

The United States is projected to reduce emissions by 1.3%, primarily because of lower coal use. Coal emissions increased in 2025 as elevated natural gas prices and cold weather encouraged greater reliance on coal.

India is moving in the opposite direction. Its fossil fuel emissions are expected to grow by 4.4% in 2026, exceeding its average annual growth rate of 3.5% over the past decade.

Elsewhere, the European Union is projected to cut emissions by 1.5%, while Japan is expected to record a 1% reduction.

Taken together, countries outside these major economies are forecast to reduce emissions by 0.7%. Much of that decrease comes from lower oil consumption, likely reflecting higher prices and restrictions on global supplies.

Oil Emissions Decline as Coal Continues to Rise

The report also provides a breakdown of projected emissions from individual fossil fuels.

Oil is expected to experience the largest reduction, with emissions falling 1.9% in 2026. Natural gas emissions are projected to decrease by 0.3%, while coal emissions are expected to increase by 0.6%.

International transportation is also contributing to the overall decline. Emissions from international aviation and international shipping are each forecast to fall by 1%. Reduced aviation activity in the Middle East is partly responsible for the decrease in air travel emissions.

Although these developments help slow fossil fuel emissions, the report indicates that much of the progress remains vulnerable to economic and geopolitical changes.

Deforestation Threatens Global Climate Progress

One of the report's most concerning findings involves carbon emissions from changes in land use.

Although emissions from land-use change have generally declined over the past decade, they are expected to increase to 5.1 billion metric tons of CO2 in 2026.

The projected rise is linked to increased peat fires (almost entirely ignited by human activities) and the degradation of forests in Southeast Asia. Drier conditions associated with the developing El Niño have contributed to these problems.

Even with the latest increase, the long-term growth of total emissions has slowed considerably. Over the past decade, combined emissions from fossil fuels and land-use change increased by an average of 0.3% annually (0.3% per year), compared with 1.7% annually during the preceding decade (1.7% per year).

Permanent deforestation remains a major source of carbon dioxide. Between 2016 and 2025, it released approximately 3.8 billion metric tons of CO2 each year. Reforestation and the establishment of new forests remove substantial amounts of carbon, but these activities offset only about half the emissions associated with permanent deforestation.

China, the 27 countries of the European Union, and the United States together account for the largest carbon removals through reforestation and afforestation, absorbing approximately 0.8 billion metric tons of CO2 annually.

Brazil, Russia, and Indonesia also absorb considerable carbon through forest growth and restoration. However, in those countries, emissions from deforestation outweigh the benefits.

Emerging technologies designed to remove carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere or through other new approaches are making only a tiny contribution. At their current scale, these methods (excluding conventional means such as reforestation) compensate for less than 30 minutes of annual fossil fuel CO2 emissions.

Meanwhile, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide is projected to reach 427.7 parts per million in 2026, approximately 54% higher than before the Industrial Revolution.

More Countries Are Growing Their Economies While Cutting Emissions

A separate analysis by the same researchers, currently in press in another peer-reviewed journal, offers additional evidence that the expansion of clean energy is changing the relationship between economic growth and carbon emissions.

As global energy demand increases, solar power, wind power, and electric vehicles can prevent some of that additional consumption from producing new fossil fuel emissions (or "offset").

Looking ahead through the end of 2028, the researchers estimate that expanding clean technologies will offset between 64% and 79% of the emissions that would otherwise result from growing energy demand.

Another encouraging trend is the increasing number of countries reducing emissions while their economies continue to expand.

According to the analysis, 59 countries had lower emissions in 2025 than in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, even as their economies grew.

The benefits are not limited to countries where emissions have already begun declining. Between 2019 and 2025, every major world region experienced slower emissions growth, including China, India, and other emerging economies where total emissions continued to rise.

Solar, Wind, and Electric Vehicles Are Reshaping Emissions

Electric vehicles are making an increasingly important contribution to reducing emissions, although their overall impact is still limited by the time required to replace existing gasoline and diesel vehicles.

In 2025, approximately 10% of the global car fleet was electrified (or 6% excluding hybrids). As more conventional vehicles are replaced, electric transportation is expected to play a larger role in reducing fossil fuel consumption.

Solar and wind power are already producing much more substantial benefits.

In 2010, these renewable energy sources prevented an estimated 0.28 billion metric tons of CO2 emissions. By 2025, that figure had climbed to 4.1 billion metric tons, and it is projected to reach 4.6 billion metric tons in 2026.

The sharp increase demonstrates how quickly cleaner electricity generation is expanding and how much additional pollution would be produced without it.

The researchers believe that continued progress could bring the world to a critical milestone sooner than many might expect.

"If further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away."

The Global Carbon Budget is compiled annually by an international collaboration of more than 140 scientists. It provides a transparent assessment of global carbon emissions using established scientific methods and undergoes peer review.

The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is scheduled for publication as a preprint in Earth System Science Data on November 10, with a peer-reviewed version to follow.

#4294. A.O.T 3 Final Preview: Possibly Shaping Up To Be One of the Best Anime Adaptation Video Games

This is DualShockers' preview of Attack on Titan 3, the penultimate entry in the AOT Video Game series developed by Omega Force and published by Koei Tecmo.

The Attack on Titan series by Hajime Isayama is genuinely one of the most important works for fans worldwide. The show has sparked a massive debate over its controversial ending, but putting that aside, you can’t argue with its overall impact: brilliant storytelling and action that fans will remember for ages.

DualShockers played A.O.T. 3 at a preview event, slashing Titans and humans alike, with the entirety of Attack on Titan's story being adapted.

And now, eight years after the last game in the franchise, Koei Tecmo’s Omega Force is back with Attack on Titan 3. The full game launches next month in December on the PS5, Xbox Series X and S, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2. At DualShockers, we had the opportunity to check out a final preview build, and I must say, as a veteran fan of both the series and the games, they’re truly going out swinging on this one.

One of the biggest changes in Attack on Titan 3 is how it approaches its storytelling. You see, back then there was this evident problem that Omega Force could only adapt parts of the story since the anime was still airing, which meant that you weren’t going to get the full package, or at least, where the manga had reached in contrast to the show.

With AOT3, it still remains true to the storytelling presentation of the prior entries. But rather than simply allowing you to relive the anime's biggest moments through the familiar cast, this game once again introduces an original character for you to create and customize.

Our OC character suffers a devastating loss after their previous squad is wiped out during a Titan encounter beyond the walls. So, after developing a fear of Titans from the incident, they're removed from active duty and assigned to instruct the 104th Cadet Corps. This gives you a chance to interact with familiar faces such as Eren, Armin, and Mikasa before eventually graduating from the instructor role and taking command of your own reconnaissance squad.

This approach is very promising because it gives Omega Force a chance to explore parts of the Attack on Titan universe that don't necessarily receive the same attention in the anime. You're not another member of Eren's generation experiencing everything alongside him. But instead, you're an experienced soldier watching these young cadets grow into the people who will eventually shape humanity's fate.

There are also original story events and character interactions designed to expand on the relationships between your character and the existing cast, which is a very nice gesture for us longtime fans if we want something new from this whole experience, especially for characters that didn’t get a ton of screen time in the main show or earlier seasons.

DualShockers spoke to A.O.T. 3 producer Hideo Suzuki about the new Titans, balancing grittiness with arcade action, and why there's no romance.

Of course, none of this hard work over the past 8 years would matter nearly as much without the one thing that makes AOT such an exciting property to adapt into a video game: its combat.

Fortunately, Omega Force hasn't simply brought back the same Omni-Directional Mobility (ODM) system from Attack on Titan 2 and called it a day. The studio has made several adjustments to how you can move around the battlefield, giving the familiar grappling mechanics far more flexibility while also adding new layers of strategy to Titan encounters.

Previously, much of the combat revolved around attaching your ODM anchors to a Titan, reeling yourself towards it, and timing your attack to strike its nape. While that foundation remains intact, AOT3 has generally put more emphasis on identifying weaknesses before committing to an attack. The gameplay rhythm now feels more like a hybrid between a strategic action game.

You can now target individual body parts, allowing you to damage limbs, interrupt attacks, and temporarily immobilize Titans before going for the finishing blow. This is especially important because these guys are much more aggressive, with new attack patterns that require you to watch their movements rather than blindly rush toward their weak spots.

One of the biggest changes in Attack on Titan 3 is how it approaches its storytelling.

Other noticeably uplifting additions include the maneuverability upgrades and defensive options. You can attach yourself to certain surfaces to reposition, use boost jumps to gain additional height, and even dive or slide along the ground to avoid incoming attacks, which is very useful when dealing with larger Titans during their one-on-one boss fight encounters where you have to stun them for the one-hit kill from their nape area.

As for defensive mechanics, you can use well-timed dodges and parries to defend against incoming attacks. Combat Arts also add another layer of progression, giving you access to powerful unlockable special attacks as you increase your military rank. It's an ambitious evolution of the combat from the prior entries, one that I’m very excited to experience to a greater extent with the full release.

The overall game’s flow looks extremely ambitious, and what I mean is that the game has three working gears in motion for the full package here: interacting with your squadmates at the base, the main story missions that progress the campaign, and your Exterior missions.

The latter is one of the highlights, as it lets you freely explore the world with your squad in tow to hunt down more Titans and fulfil different requests from NPCs you come across. It’s essentially a way to give you more gameplay freedom instead of railroading you from start to finish to showcase the anime's main story, and doing Exterior missions also lets you reap additional rewards and useful upgrade materials, which you definitely need and can’t skip since they let you enhance your equipment.

And speaking of gameplay freedom, you can put any doubts to rest about whether you can jump into this game without prior experience with how the first two games worked. There are a bunch of accessibility and control scheme options that let any player easily enjoy the story, but if you want total control, you can turn off any options that automate the combat mechanics, which I honestly prefer since you’re way more vulnerable to mistakes that way, and it makes the game more punishing.

Still, I can promise you that Attack on Titan 3 is genuinely worth having on your radar for the December releases. With how much I got to sample here, I can’t wait to see how more of the character interactions play out, how the talent points fully work with everything in place, along with how the noteworthy battles in the show play out here, and that includes the whole sections of Marley from Season 4 and beyond. It is a lot to look forward to on my side, but I’ll gladly march into battle head-on with my goth Scout Corps Captain.

This list discusses the best Anime-inspired action games that capture the genre far better than SAO: Echoes of Aincrad.

#4292. Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide important clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

The results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

"Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an important question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," said corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death

The researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

People classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," said Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

Because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

This extended timeline was especially important because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

This creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

The researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

One possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

"Nutrition can be a big problem for people with dementia," said Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves."

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

Materials provided by Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4291. Invictus Gaming beat Top Esports 3-1 to reach first Worlds semi-final since 2019

Invictus Gaming knocked out fellow LPL side Top Esports in the opening quarter-final of Worlds 2026 in Allen, Texas. The result guarantees China a semi-final place after the LPL's 0-4 start in the Swiss Stage.

Invictus Gaming are through to the last four of Worlds 2026. They beat fellow LPL side Top Esports in the opening match of the Knockout Stage. The series was played at the Credit Union of Texas Event Center in Allen, Texas, on 3 November (US time).

The win guarantees China a semi-final place. That matters after the LPL’s 0-4 start in the Swiss Stage. IG now meet either Gen.G or LYON. Gen.G beat IG 1-0 in the Swiss Stage and finished it with a perfect 3-0 record.

TES played the event without ZUIAN. On 6 October the club announced that Bai ‘369’ Jia-Hao would move into the starting line-up because of visa problems affecting ZUIAN.

The stand-in still made his mark. IG won Game 1 after building a gold lead of more than 10,000. TES levelled in Game 2 when 369, on Renekton, killed JiaQi and TheShy on his own late in the game. IG then took the next two games to close out the series.

Every Knockout Stage match is a single-elimination best-of-five played with Fearless Draft. The two sides knew each other well. They met twice in best-of-five series in September. IG won 3-2 in the LPL Split 3 playoffs on 5 September. TES won 3-1 in the LPL Regional Finals on 17 September.

The prize money gap is now fixed. Worlds 2026 has a total prize pool of US$5,000,000, with US$1,000,000 for the winner. Each losing semi-finalist receives US$400,000, so IG are guaranteed at least that sum.

IG’s run began with a mid-season rescue. The team started LPL Split 3 in the Nirvana Group. The club then asked TheShy and Rookie, who were both on a break, to come back. The pair helped the side qualify for Worlds. Both won the 2018 world title with IG.

TheShy said he had promised IG’s CEO he would help if asked. “I came back to keep my word,” he said after the series.

The #Worlds2026 Knockout Stage bracket after today's match! pic.twitter.com/iaPQndNZSW

— LoL Esports (@lolesports) November 4, 2026

The rest of the quarter-finals follow this week. Gen.G play LYON on 4 November. Dplus KIA face Bilibili Gaming on 5 November. Europe’s last team, Karmine Corp, play T1 on 6 November. All three start at 16:00 CT.

The semi-finals will be played in Allen on 7 and 8 November. The final will be held in Brooklyn on Saturday 14 November at 2pm EST.

#4290. NASA offers $500,000 to develop next-generation electric rocket engines

NASA is offering $500,000 in prizes to encourage American companies to develop more capable electric propulsion systems for future space missions. The competition focuses on a technology known as Hall effect thrusters, which use electricity to propel spacecraft through space.

The new initiative, called the Advanced Mid-Power Electric Rocket (AMPERE) Challenge, seeks to advance mid-power (3-7 kW) propulsion systems. Government agencies and aerospace industry experts have identified this class of thrusters as an important technology for satellite operations, national defense, and space exploration.

By inviting commercial companies to design and demonstrate working prototypes, NASA hopes to accelerate progress in electric propulsion and help prepare promising technologies for practical use.

Unlike conventional rockets, which burn chemical propellants to produce powerful bursts of thrust, electric propulsion systems use electrical energy to accelerate charged particles and expel them at high speeds. The resulting force pushes a spacecraft in the opposite direction.

Hall effect thrusters are a particular type of electric propulsion system that uses electric and magnetic fields to control and accelerate charged particles. They typically produce much less thrust than chemical rocket engines, but they can use propellant far more efficiently.

That efficiency makes electric thrusters especially valuable for missions that require spacecraft to operate for extended periods. Rather than delivering a brief, powerful push, these engines can provide gentle acceleration over long stretches of time, gradually changing a spacecraft's speed or trajectory.

Hall effect thrusters are already used in space, including for adjusting satellite orbits and maintaining spacecraft positions. Improving their performance could expand the range of missions they can support.

The power range targeted by NASA's challenge refers to the electrical energy these systems consume. A kilowatt equals 1,000 watts, so the competition focuses on thrusters that operate using approximately 3,000 to 7,000 watts of electrical power.

NASA Seeks More Advanced Spacecraft Thrusters

The AMPERE Challenge is designed to help American companies move promising electric propulsion concepts beyond early development and toward technologies that can be evaluated under realistic testing conditions.

Participating companies will develop and demonstrate Hall-effect thruster prototypes within the specified power range. NASA intends to assess their performance using its testing facilities, providing an opportunity to evaluate how well the systems function and identify areas that need improvement.

This testing is an important step in turning experimental propulsion technology into equipment suitable for future missions. Spacecraft engines must deliver predictable performance and operate reliably in the demanding environment of space.

By supporting commercial innovation, NASA aims to strengthen the technological foundation for future government and private sector missions. Potential applications include satellite operations, defense systems, and robotic exploration beyond Earth.

$500,000 in Prizes for Electric Propulsion Innovation

NASA has allocated a total of $500,000 in cash prizes for the AMPERE Challenge. The competition will take place across three phases, with as many as two winning teams eligible to receive up to $250,000 each.

In addition to the financial awards, winning teams can gain access to NASA testing resources and technology. These opportunities could help companies evaluate and improve their propulsion systems while advancing their readiness for future applications.

The challenge is open to commercial companies that are incorporated in the United States and maintain their primary place of business in the country.

Registration begins November 9, 2026, and closes January 27, 2027.

Companies interested in participating can find complete competition rules, eligibility requirements, and registration information on the official NASA AMPERE Challenge website.

Through this competition, NASA hopes to encourage new advances in electric rocket technology and strengthen the propulsion capabilities available for the next generation of spacecraft.

#4289. 10 Best Soulslikes With Fluid Movement Mechanics

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Soulslikes represent a subgenre of ARPGs with quite distinct characteristics, including various constraints intended to establish their aggressive and challenging nature.

Features such as combat that prioritize functionality over spectacle, as well as limited and mundane traversal methods, are a constant among Soulsborne games' descendants, precisely because they exploit these limitations to create immersive experiences.

It's an incredibly delicate balance because, if poorly executed, it leads to clunky campaigns where the mere act of moving from one place to another can become tedious, though there are also exceptions that prove the rule.

Therefore, in order to shed light on these anomalies and draw on the contributions of titles with a lighter approach to the genre, here are the ten best Soulslikes with fluid movement mechanics.

Since I first played it, I think I've been one of Elden Ring Nightreign's most fervent critics, as it's a title that constantly contradicts me to the point of including it in a list of Soulslikes despite being developed by FromSoftware.

However, if there's one thing I not only can't complain about, but which I sincerely find masterful within the genre, it's the way it agilizes movement to a maximum. It gives each playthrough a dynamism uncommon in the genre.

Thanks to the characters' speed, their ability to climb walls, the spirit streams to jump to incredible heights, and the Spectral Hawk flight, which allows you to hover over areas with remarkable accuracy regarding your landing spot, simply wandering around is quite satisfying—a statement I can't make about almost any other title of this kind.

Is it cheating to include a game from the original influences' roots, which is also more of a roguelite, in this list? Perhaps, yet this is the first time the study has taken movement so seriously, so it deserves the mention.

Phantom Blade Zero is a fusion of traditional action-adventure elements with ideas borrowed from both Soulslikes and Metroidvanias, creating an extravagant yet highly satisfying cocktail.

The game boasts a staggering array of flashy weapons whose visual grandeur is breathtaking, especially in the hands of an ultra-powerful protagonist who is capable of putting those tools at the movement's mercy.

With the ability to sprint at high speed, swing on chains to cross gaps, run along walls, and use a grappling hook to reach high points, this title refuses to simply block doors on one side but instead strives to add depth to the exploration.

Unfortunately, most of these mechanics are prompts that can only be activated at specific, controlled locations, but they are more than enough to make Phantom Blade Zero a more dynamic game than average in this regard.

If you’re looking for the best FromSoftware-inspired ARPGs, I recommend the best Soulslikes based on critics' scores.

Speaking of middle ground, Nine Sols takes Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice's combat system and Hollow Knight's perspective, platforming, and exploration to create one of the decade's most wonderful indie games.

While it leans towards one or the other inspiration depending on the context, it's incredible how Yi soars across the maps once you've unlocked all of his movement tools, which are simple in concept but incredibly rewarding in execution.

Surely, it's nothing more than double jumps, dashes, and kicking enemies' skulls to get airborne, but it's enough to perfectly complement his prodigious combat mechanics.

Even if Nine Sols had terrible traversal, it would still be great because of how it shines in all the other elements, making the polished movement mechanics all the more admirable.

Especially considering it was released when Soulslikes were still in their infancy, Salt and Sanctuary was a major surprise, perfectly adapting the genre's formula to the 2D side-scrolling perspective.

With a wealth of secrets hidden behind the movement abilities you progressively unlock, it's a title that knows how to make platforming satisfying and imbue it with meaning beyond simply moving from point A to point B.

When you first change the gravity orientation, for example, you realize Salt and Sanctuary isn't just a great action RPG with challenging bosses and outstanding worldbuilding, but a game that understood that part of the Dark Souls trilogy's charm lay in how it transformed each new tool into a way to reinterpret the levels.

Years have passed, and I still believe it's the purest and most outstanding 2D Soulslike among those that don't venture too far into other genres, as few have captured the essence of their inspiration as well as this one.

Team Ninja is among the developers that have placed the most emphasis on the Soulslike genre, and while Rise of the Ronin isn't their most outstanding iteration, it certainly stands out when movement is the key factor.

Based on its open-world concept, the game boasts one of the most inventive arrays of traversal tools the genre has ever seen, offering a horse, a grappling hook, and a glider to facilitate the discovery of its expansive map.

If you compare it to direct peers like Ghost of Tsushima, it might fall short, but if the conversation turns to previous titles from the studio, such as Nioh, or games from FromSoftware, like the aforementioned Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, the tone shifts.

Ultimately, Rise of the Ronin combines a myriad of ideas that will appeal to some and deter others, though the fact that it brings with it a form of exploration that avoids relying solely on walking and fast travel is undeniable.

If you’re still waiting for the next FromSoftware game, check out these ten Soulslikes that most people haven’t played but definitely should.

Shattered - Tale of the Forgotten King is a fascinating title due to its attempt, although often erratic, to combine 3D combat with side-scrolling platforming, which is a unique approach even outside Soulslikes' spaces.

The combat is present and functional enough to sustain the experience for the hours it lasts, yet what truly catches the eye is the movement, as it feels like Journey thanks to its flow and smoothness.

In addition to its perspective shifts, which alternate between combat and 2.5D traversal, moving through its open world on a hoverboard feels compelling, mainly because of how unexpected it is to encounter such a mechanic in this type of game.

Indeed, there isn't much to do once you're in free-roaming areas, but since this article focuses on movement mechanics, Shattered - Tale of the Forgotten King keeps its place among the most distinguished in the genre.

While the first game in the series was pure action-adventure, and the second shifted towards open-world RPG elements, Darksiders 3 changed course once again, this time aiming to be both a Soulslike and a Metroidvania.

By merging the level design and combat system of the former with the progression and backtracking mechanics of the latter, Gunfire Games created a phenomenal symphony that truly draws on its hack-and-slash heritage.

Darksiders 3 embraces grandeur, allowing you to transform into diverse avatars to double jump and burn through barriers, glide on air currents, become an energy ball to cling to walls, or even walk on water.

If you add to all these different ways of traversing the use of Fury's whip to swing from platform to platform, the only logical conclusion left to draw is that Darksiders 3 is a marvel when it comes to moving around.

Another Crab's Treasure is among the most creatively designed Soulslikes we've had the pleasure of enjoying this decade, and its movement mechanics are anything but an exception.

The game's levels are extremely vertical and branching, so it needed movement methods that could handle its demanding platforming sections with jumps, climbs, glides, and directional grappling hooks that take you from one ledge to another in a matter of seconds.

It's no wonder the game has become a favorite among speedrunners; its open areas combined with its fluid maneuverability create the perfect breeding ground for exploring the limits of gravity and Krill's stamina.

It has incredible bosses, extensive customization, a remarkable audiovisual component, strong thematic cohesion... Another Crab's Treasure is a complete package, and thankfully, Aggro Crab didn't leave platforming out of the equation.

If you're looking for community-endorsed experiences, I recommend you try these ten Soulslikes where the user score is higher than the critic score.

After Hollow Knight established the Soulslite variant as an alternative for those who didn't want to fully commit to the formula, Hollow Knight: Silksong further solidified its fresh take on the genre.

The loss of resources upon death, save points that also serve as locations to modify your character, pattern-based bosses, cryptic lore... We all know the points of convergence, but where it truly breaks away is in its movement.

Even when compared to pure platformers, Hollow Knight: Silksong possesses a unique grace when it comes to traversal, with an incredibly agile Hornet who's capable of using her abilities in unique ways to facilitate her journey through Pharloom.

Grabbing ledges, bouncing off environmental elements, flying on air currents, leaping between walls, using your needle to propel yourself forward... The array of abilities available during the game is incredible and, above all, very satisfying, especially when you learn to chain them together and run without anything or anyone stopping you.

Nevertheless, beyond the games made by FromSoftware itself or titles that only tangentially touch on the genre, the purest example of a Soulslike with the most fluid movement mechanics is Valor Mortis.

Coming from Ghostrunner, One More Level leveraged its undeniable aptitude for first-person platforming and created an entire world around it, giving us an adventure where you jump, dash, swoop, and grapple with impressive ease.

Valor Mortis is already a striking project for its combination of such divergent concepts as stealth, first-person shooting, and ARPG combat based on parries, though adding such natural platforming sections on top of all that is simply incredible.

I spent the entire campaign amazed by the simple fact that Soulslikes don't move this fast and seamlessly, much less in sequences where you're speeding around in a minecart or running across platforms that are collapsing because a giant monster is attacking you with its tentacles.

Valor Mortis is a game that can be criticized for many things, but not for its movement. In fact, this is an area where it excels so much that other games should strive to emulate its talent.

From the indie ecosystem to productions approaching AAA measures, these are ten Soulslike franchises that should come back by 2027.

#4287. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers

One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

#4286. Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

New preliminary research involving more than 440,000 American adults has uncovered a concerning association between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke. The findings suggest that even occasional marijuana use may be linked to higher odds of cardiovascular problems, raising new questions about the health effects of a substance that is becoming increasingly common across the United States.

The research, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, found that the association was not limited to people who frequently used cannabis. It also appeared across different methods of consumption (smoked or edible, etc.). Researchers emphasized that cannabis use should be considered when discussing heart health and stroke prevention.

Scientific Sessions 2026 took place November 6 through 9 in Chicago, bringing together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, clinical advances, and emerging evidence.

Cannabis refers to the plant itself, while marijuana is a commonly used term for cannabis products containing enough THC to produce psychoactive effects.

Marijuana Use Is Rising Across the United States

"Previous research has indicated that cannabis use is rapidly increasing in the United States, with 1 in 6 adults in 2024 reporting having used it within the last month, up from 1 in 10 in 2020 -- a 51% increase," said study author Aabha Divya, M.B.B.S., M.Ch., an assistant professor in the division of cardiothoracic surgery at the Tulane University School of Medicine in New Orleans.

Earlier research conducted between 2016 and 2020 had already identified associations between cannabis consumption and unfavorable cardiovascular outcomes. Those findings also suggested that using cannabis more frequently during a given month was connected to greater cardiovascular risk.

However, the evidence has not always been consistent. With recreational marijuana becoming legal in more places and cannabis products increasingly available, Divya and colleagues wanted to investigate these possible health effects in a larger population.

"We wanted to expand on this earlier work because cannabis use has become increasingly common in the United States, as recreational legalization and commercial availability of various products with cannabis have also expanded. Previous studies have raised concerns about possible cardiovascular effects; however, the results have not been consistent," Divya said.

The researchers examined information collected through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), a large telephone survey of American adults. They combined responses from jurisdictions that collected information about cannabis consumption between 2020 and 2024.

Participants answered questions about their marijuana use and whether a healthcare professional had ever diagnosed them with cardiovascular conditions, including a heart attack, stroke, or coronary heart disease.

Even Occasional Marijuana Use Was Linked to Higher Stroke Odds

One of the most striking findings was that infrequent cannabis use was associated with cardiovascular problems. In fact, the researchers did not find the steady increase in cardiovascular risk with more frequent use that they had expected.

The analysis revealed several important associations:

These findings were unexpected because the relationship between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease did not consistently become stronger as consumption increased.

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward. We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease," Divya said.

Although the study cannot establish that marijuana directly causes strokes or other cardiovascular conditions, the findings suggest that occasional consumption should not automatically be considered free of potential cardiovascular concerns.

"As cannabis use becomes more common, it is increasingly important that people and their healthcare professionals include it in conversations about cardiovascular health, just as they discuss tobacco, alcohol and other commonly used substances," she added.

Experts Urge Greater Attention to Cannabis and Heart Health

Robert L. Page II, Pharm.D., M.S.P.H., FAHA, who led the writing group responsible for the American Heart Association's 2020 cannabis scientific statement, said the findings add to growing concerns about marijuana's possible cardiovascular effects.

One challenge in evaluating those effects is that many cannabis users also smoke tobacco. Because tobacco is already an established cardiovascular risk factor, separating its effects from those of cannabis can be difficult.

Page, who was not involved in the research, explained why the new findings deserve attention.

"Unfortunately, many patients who use cannabis may also smoke tobacco, which completely clouds the issue when addressing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk. In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case. This is the second observational study to suggest that cannabis exposure (without tobacco smoking) may be a potential risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease. Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events. To this end, clinicians should be addressing cannabis use with their patients as they would tobacco use when considering the risk of cardiovascular disease."

Page is a professor in the department of clinical pharmacy and the department of physical medicine/rehabilitation at the University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences in Aurora, Colorado.

How Researchers Studied Nearly Half a Million Americans

The analysis included 442,906 adults living in the United States (average age of 49 years; approximately half women). Their responses came from telephone surveys conducted through the BRFSS.

Researchers used survey information collected from 2020 through 2024, focusing on states that had included an optional marijuana questionnaire. Between 16 and 24 states participated in this portion of the survey each year, meaning the analysis did not represent every state.

Participants reported how many days they had consumed cannabis during the preceding month. The questions covered multiple ways of using marijuana (smoking, vaping or ingesting gummies or other cannabis-containing foods).

The researchers divided participants into four categories based on their reported use:

Participants also indicated whether they had ever received a diagnosis of heart attack, heart disease, heart-related chest pain, or stroke.

To better distinguish the association with cannabis from other potential explanations, the researchers accounted for numerous established cardiovascular risk factors. These included demographic characteristics, tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, physical inactivity, education, and income.

Why the Findings Do Not Prove Marijuana Causes Strokes

Despite the large number of participants, the study has several limitations that affect how its findings should be interpreted.

First, the analysis examined associations between reported cannabis use and previously diagnosed cardiovascular conditions at a single point in time. This means researchers could not determine whether marijuana use preceded the cardiovascular problems or whether it directly contributed to them.

The information also depended on participants accurately recalling and reporting their cannabis consumption and medical histories (making them subject to potential errors in memory). Such reports may not always reflect actual patterns of use or diagnoses.

Another limitation was the lack of information about the strength of the cannabis products participants consumed or the quantities they used. Without those details, the researchers could not evaluate whether THC potency or the amount consumed influenced the observed associations.

The researchers also acknowledged that some participants may have reduced or discontinued cannabis consumption after being diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. As a result, the group reporting no cannabis use in the previous month may have included former users.

These uncertainties make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how consumption frequency affects cardiovascular health. Nevertheless, the findings add to growing evidence that cannabis use deserves closer examination as a possible factor in heart disease and stroke.

As marijuana becomes more widely available and its use continues to increase, researchers and healthcare professionals are emphasizing the importance of discussing cannabis alongside other substances that may affect cardiovascular health.

#4284. PlayStation Adds Major Feature to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, ARC Raiders, and More

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

A big component of what makes the PS5 an attractive console, besides just being able to play particular games you can’t play elsewhere, is the console’s various built-in graphical perks. Since the PS5 first launched in 2020, its hardware power has remained one of its definitive perks, with the PS5 Pro in particular taking matters further with the inclusion of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution, better known as PSSR.

In this list, we discuss some of the best PS4 games to play with the PS5 Pro's Image Quality Enhancements option.

Even though the PS5 already has a few years under its belt, the brand isn’t just resting on its proverbial laurels and letting its existing hardware carry it. New advancements in graphical technology are coming out all the time, and even games that looked pretty stunning when they first dropped like Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 can always look a little bit better.

To that end, PlayStation has added support for one of its up-and-coming graphical frameworks, Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), to several more games in the PS5’s library following its initial launch last month exclusively in Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei. The newly-upscaled games include Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, Control Resonant, ARC Raiders, The Finals, No Man’s Sky, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam.

In case you forgot, QSSR is a proprietary AI upscaling framework created in tandem between PlayStation and AMD. This framework came about from Project Amethyst, an ongoing developmental effort between both companies that also gave rise to PSSR. According to the official announcement of the newly-upscaled games on the official PlayStation news blog, QSSR provides “sharper details, cleaner edges, and more stable images than traditional upscalers,” and since it’s built on the same platform as PSSR, it’s easy for games that already use that framework to incorporate it.

QSSR is a proprietary AI upscaling framework created in tandem between PlayStation and AMD.

In that news post, PlayStation got quotes from all of the improved games’ developers on how QSSR has affected their respective titles. Insomniac Games’ Mike Fitzgerald said that, after incorporating the tech into the launch of Marvel’s Wolverine, the studio decided to go back and add it to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 as well. “We’re excited for players to swing back into our 2023 title and see QSSR’s exciting image stability and sharpness benefits in both Fidelity and Performance modes,” he said.

Sony has introduced a brand-new AI-powered upscaling technology called Quick Spectral Super Resolution.

Remedy Entertainment’s Erik Jansson said that “QSSR gives Control Resonant a much more stable and detailed image, and we’ve worked closely with Sony to have it ready in an update coming in December.”

Embark Studios’ Mikael Linderholm said that QSSR support will be coming soon to ARC Raiders and The Finals, and said that his studio is “very happy to see Sony’s continued investment in PlayStation technology translate into meaningful improvements for all players.”

While I’m personally of the belief that graphics alone don’t automatically make a game good, it is still pretty interesting to see the degree to which graphical fidelity can be improved, especially as we start to run up against the proverbial limits of realism.

Obviously, the use of AI in games is a feisty topic, particularly in presentation elements like voice acting. In the specific use case of graphics, some efforts like NVIDIA’s AI-powered DLSS5 and its widely-mocked “yassify filter” on character models is probably not the optimal way to be going about this. Rather than trying to generate and overwrite existing graphics with slop, something like QSSR is closer to the ideal, taking what’s already present and merely smoothing out the rougher edges of the environmental rendering process.

PlayStation has promised that this tech will be coming to more games, ending its news post by saying, “Developers are just getting started, and we’re excited to keep working with them to bring QSSR to more games on PS5 in the coming months.”

Two classic apocalyptic shooters have received free modern graphical facelifts.

#4283. Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.

The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.

Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health

The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.

Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.

A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).

However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.

Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.

"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."

FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events

To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.

The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.

Several differences stood out in the analysis:

These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.

"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.

Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable

One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.

Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.

How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.

These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.

Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?

Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.

"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."

Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.

Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.

How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports

The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.

Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.

Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).

Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.

The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.

Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.

Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.
